cls: Water-soluble vitamin (vitamin B3 amide form; NAD/NADP precursor)
pharm: The amide form of vitamin B3 (niacinamide), a precursor of the coenzymes NAD and NADP that are essential for cellular oxidation-reduction reactions and energy metabolism. Unlike nicotinic acid, it does not cause flushing and does not lower lipids; used to treat/prevent niacin deficiency (pellagra) and as a dermatologic agent.

summary: Nicotinamide (niacinamide) is the amide form of vitamin B3. It is converted to the coenzymes NAD and NADP, which are required by more than 400 enzymes for oxidation-reduction reactions and cellular energy metabolism. It is used to prevent and treat niacin deficiency (pellagra) and is contained in many multivitamin and supplement preparations. Unlike nicotinic acid (niacin), nicotinamide does NOT cause cutaneous flushing and does NOT have lipid-lowering effects, so it cannot substitute for niacin in dyslipidemia. For pellagra, a typical regimen is about 300 mg/day orally in divided doses (or about 100 mg/day parenterally) for 3-4 weeks. It is generally very safe at recommended doses; hepatotoxicity is seen mainly at very high doses (often cited above 3 g/day). It has recognized dermatologic uses, including oral nicotinamide to reduce new non-melanoma skin cancers in high-risk patients and as a treatment adjunct in some bullous and acne disorders.

Dietary supplementation as a source of vitamin B3

moa: Nicotinamide is incorporated into nicotinamide adenine dinucleotide (NAD) and its phosphorylated form NADP, the principal electron-carrier coenzymes for hundreds of oxidoreductase reactions involved in glycolysis, the citric acid cycle, oxidative phosphorylation, and other anabolic/catabolic pathways. Adequate NAD/NADP is essential for cellular energy production and tissue integrity; deficiency produces pellagra (dermatitis, diarrhea, dementia). Nicotinamide also inhibits poly(ADP-ribose) polymerase (PARP) and modulates cellular energy/DNA-repair pathways, which underlies its investigated dermatologic and photoprotective effects. Unlike nicotinic acid, it does not act on the GPR109A receptor and therefore does not cause flushing or alter lipid metabolism.

relative: Use of very high (multi-gram) doses in patients with hepatic impairment
monitor: Liver function when high doses are used
Glycemic control (high doses may affect glucose tolerance)

preg: Nicotinamide is a required nutrient and is considered safe at recommended dietary/therapeutic doses during pregnancy; adequate B3 intake is needed for normal development. Avoid unnecessary very high doses.
lact: Nicotinamide is present in breast milk as a normal nutrient and is considered safe at recommended doses during breastfeeding.
renal: No specific dose adjustment is required at usual doses. Use caution with very high doses; the tolerable upper intake limits set by regulatory bodies should not be routinely exceeded.
hepatic: At recommended doses nicotinamide is well tolerated. Hepatotoxicity has been reported mainly at very high doses (commonly cited above 3 g/day); avoid such doses in hepatic impairment and monitor liver function if high-dose therapy is used.

moderate: Carbamazepine and primidone - nicotinamide may raise their plasma levels (reported)
minor: High doses may affect glucose tolerance and glycemic control
interactions.food: May be taken with food; no clinically significant food interaction at usual doses.
interactions.alcohol: Chronic excessive alcohol use is a common cause of niacin/B3 deficiency and pellagra; limiting alcohol supports repletion.
interactions.diagnostics: Very high doses may interfere with some urinary catecholamine assays and glucose measurements; no significant interference at usual doses.

serious: Impaired glucose tolerance at high doses
emergency: Severe hepatotoxicity from very high doses (jaundice, marked transaminase elevation)

monitoring: Resolution of pellagra signs (dermatitis, diarrhea, neurologic/cognitive symptoms)
Liver function tests if high doses are used
Glycemic control if high doses are used in patients with diabetes
counsel: This is the amide form of vitamin B3 - unlike plain niacin it does not cause flushing
It does not lower cholesterol, so it cannot replace niacin if that is why niacin was prescribed
Take as directed; very high doses (grams per day) are not needed and can affect the liver
If you have pellagra, also improve your diet and take it for the full course
Tell your doctor if you have liver disease or diabetes before taking high doses
pk: Rapidly absorbed orally; pellagra symptoms improve over days to weeks
Readily absorbed from the GI tract
Short - rapidly distributed and converted to NAD/NADP; excess excreted in urine as metabolites
Body pool maintained by daily intake; dosed daily/divided
Store at room temperature, protected from light and moisture
pearls: Nicotinamide (niacinamide) is the amide of vitamin B3 and a precursor of NAD/NADP coenzymes
Key difference from nicotinic acid: NO flushing and NO lipid-lowering effect
Pellagra (the 3 Ds - dermatitis, diarrhea, dementia) responds to ~300 mg/day orally in divided doses for 3-4 weeks
Generally very safe; hepatotoxicity is mainly a concern at very high doses (>3 g/day)
Oral nicotinamide 500 mg twice daily has been shown to reduce new non-melanoma skin cancers in high-risk patients (ONTRAC)
Chronic alcohol use, malabsorption, isoniazid, and carcinoid syndrome are common causes of deficiency
missed: If you miss a dose, take it when you remember. If it is almost time for the next dose, skip the missed dose and continue your regular schedule. Do not take a double dose.
overdose: Acute overdose of nicotinamide is unlikely to be serious at typical doses. Very high (multi-gram) intake may cause gastrointestinal upset and, with chronic high dosing, hepatotoxicity and impaired glucose tolerance. Management is to stop the supplement and provide supportive care, with liver function assessment if a large amount was taken.
